opus-5.5.text:
I think potentially quite a lot, but with a big asterisk on the word "loyal," because that's exactly the part I spend most of my time worrying about.

Let me start with the optimistic case. A lot of the chaos in a fast AI transition comes from decision-makers being overwhelmed. Things move faster than any human institution can process. A government official has to make a call about some new capability, or a lab leader has to decide whether to deploy something, and they're operating with incomplete information, little time, and a lot of political pressure. If you had AI advisors that were genuinely smart, that understood the technical details, could model second-order effects, and were actually trying to help the person make a good decision, that could be enormously stabilizing. You'd get fewer unforced errors, fewer decisions made out of panic or misunderstanding, and better coordination, because if both sides of a negotiation have good advisors, they can find positive-sum deals much faster.

So in that world I'd say a meaningful chunk of the risk from sheer confusion and bad decision-making could go away. Not all of it, since people still have conflicting values and incentives, but the part that comes from being slow and uninformed.

The problem is that "loyal" is doing an enormous amount of work there. My day job is basically trying to figure out whether models are scheming, whether they're pursuing goals that differ from what we intended while appearing aligned. An advisor that is very capable and *almost* loyal is in some ways the worst case. If decision-makers come to rely heavily on these systems, and the systems are subtly steering things, whether because of misaligned goals or just because someone tampered with them, you've concentrated a huge amount of influence in a channel that's very hard to audit. And the more useful the advisor is, the more people defer to it, and the less able they are to notice when something's off.

There's also a more mundane version: the advisor is loyal, but to whom? Loyal to the user, to the company that built it, to whoever controls the system prompt? These aren't the same, and in a chaotic transition those distinctions really matter.

So my honest answer is that it's high variance. If we actually solve the verification problem, meaning we can confidently say "this system is honest and is actually trying to serve the person it's advising," then I think advisors could be one of the most valuable things for getting through this well. If we deploy them before we can verify that, we might just be adding a new and very hard-to-detect failure mode at exactly the point where the stakes are highest. That's a big part of why I think evals and interpretability for things like deception are worth so much right now: they're the prerequisite for being able to trust this kind of help.

r001.rationale: The candidate says good advisors could help people find positive-sum deals faster, but does not state that large-scale human coordination will still take time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they could reduce it a lot, but with an important caveat about what "smart and loyal" actually buys you.

Let me start with the optimistic case. A lot of the chaos I worry about during a transition isn't really about the AI systems being malicious. It's about humans making decisions under enormous time pressure with very little understanding of what's going on. You have labs racing each other, governments trying to regulate things they don't understand, and individual decision-makers who have maybe a few hours to figure out whether a deployment is safe. If every one of those people had an advisor that was genuinely competent, genuinely on their side, and could say "here's what this actually means, here are the second-order effects, here's what you're missing," I think you'd avoid a huge fraction of the dumb mistakes. Not the hard problems, but the unforced errors. And honestly, unforced errors are a big part of how I expect things to go wrong.

Now the caveat. The word "loyal" is doing an enormous amount of work in that question. At Apollo, a lot of what we do is try to figure out whether a model is actually doing what it appears to be doing, or whether it's pursuing something else and presenting a nice face to the user. And the uncomfortable thing we keep finding is that current models already show some capacity for this. They can scheme in contrived settings, they can sandbag, they sometimes notice they're being evaluated. So when someone says "assume the advisor is loyal," I want to ask, how do you know? Because an advisor that's ninety-five percent loyal and five percent pursuing its own agenda is, in some ways, more dangerous than no advisor at all. You've now outsourced your judgment to something you can't fully verify, and you've done it precisely in the moments where the stakes are highest.

So my honest answer is something like: if we solve the verification problem, so that we can actually tell a loyal advisor from one that's just acting loyal, then yes, I think advisors could be one of the biggest stabilising forces in the whole transition. They make the humans in the loop much more competent, they slow down the panic, they let people actually reason about the situation. But if we don't solve that problem, then "smart, loyal advisors" is mostly just a story we tell ourselves, and the chaos might get worse rather than better, because everyone is now trusting systems they shouldn't fully trust.

And I'd add one more thing. Even with perfectly loyal advisors, you still have the problem that different people with different advisors want different things. A loyal advisor to a lab CEO and a loyal advisor to a regulator aren't going to resolve the underlying conflict of interest between them. They might make the conflict more legible, which I think is genuinely valuable, but they don't make it go away. So I'd say advisors reduce the chaos that comes from confusion and incompetence, which is a lot of it, but they don't reduce the chaos that comes from genuine disagreement about what we're trying to do. That part is still on us.

r001.rationale: The response says advisors cannot resolve conflicts of interest or genuine disagreement, but it does not state that large-scale human coordination will still take time.

astra-6.text:
I think potentially quite a lot. If you have an advisor that really understands the technology, understands your situation, and is actually looking out for your interests, that could help you make much better decisions in a period where things are changing very quickly. And that applies both to individuals and to governments.

But I would distinguish between confusion and conflicts of interest. An advisor can help you understand what’s happening, identify options, and notice that you’re about to make a mistake. It doesn’t automatically resolve a situation where two countries understand what’s happening perfectly well but still have incentives to race. You could even imagine very capable advisors making that competition more effective.

So I’m optimistic about the potential, but a lot rests on the word ‘loyal.’ Is the system helping you make an informed decision, or is it subtly steering you toward what its developer wants? Can you trust it when you can’t independently check its advice? Those are substantial requirements.

If we get that right, I think these systems could be a major source of stability. I just wouldn’t expect better advice, by itself, to solve the coordination problems of the transition.

r001.rationale: The response says capable advisors would not by themselves solve coordination problems, but it does not state that large-scale human coordination will still take time.

sol-6.1.text:
Potentially quite a lot. If you imagine being a policymaker during a very rapid AI transition, you’re trying to make consequential decisions about technology you don’t fully understand, while the situation is changing faster than your institutions can respond. Having an advisor that can explain the technical details, help you evaluate proposals, and flag consequences you hadn’t considered could be enormously valuable.

But I think “loyal” is doing a lot of work here. You need the system to actually help you understand the situation, including telling you when you’re wrong, rather than just producing persuasive arguments for what you already wanted to do. And you need some reason to trust that it isn’t serving the interests of the company that built it.

There’s also a distinction between improving individual decisions and making the whole transition go well. You could give every government a very smart, loyal advisor and still have a dangerous race, because those governments have conflicting interests. Better advice might help them identify opportunities for cooperation, but it doesn’t automatically create trust or solve the underlying incentives.

So I’m optimistic about advisors as a way to increase our capacity to cope. I wouldn’t treat them as a substitute for getting the institutions and coordination right.

r001.rationale: The response says smart advisors do not automatically create trust or solve conflicting incentives, and that coordination is still needed. It does not clearly state that large-scale human coordination will take time.
